name: Priya Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We are not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this interview is confidential. What does your day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and manage the allocation team at a large home-goods retailer. Our six planners decide how many lamps, rugs and kettles go to each store, then deal with the angry calls when stock is stranded in the wrong place. I earned an MBA and get paid well because I have turned bad forecasts around twice; I use AI tools every day to compare store sales, but I make the final order call.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, who is a freelance sound engineer. We have eleven months of household expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar planning jobs in this city. My partner’s contracts swing from month to month, so I like the cushion even with my higher salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my planners AI Plateau sounds like the tools we already use becoming a bit tidier. We should still check actual shelf space before an algorithm sends forty more lamps to a full store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel secure in my job. If change is small, my work remains deciding what to do with exceptions that forecasts miss. I would still watch my partner’s freelance bookings, because that income moves for reasons unrelated to AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d continue our Thursday store calls and use the existing AI dashboard to flag odd sales jumps. When a minor new feature appears, I’d test it against last winter’s overstock cases before changing an order rule. I’d keep our usual savings transfer each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A cleaner screen is welcome, and we have room if a freelance contract slips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which store would you call first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our smallest branch has half the shelf space that our database assumes. Its manager once stacked kettles in the staff room for three weeks. I would ask for a photo before sending another pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your partner share your calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner is less relaxed about an empty calendar, even when we have savings. I show the account balance, and we decide together which jobs are worth taking. My own role feels steady in this picture.

say: **AI Plateau** would make familiar tools a little tidier.
Store managers still need to confirm **shelf space** before new stock ships.
think: My allocation job looks **secure** when changes stay small.
My partner’s **freelance bookings** remain variable for other reasons.
do: **Continue** Thursday store calls and review unusual sales jumps.
**Test** a minor feature against last winter’s overstock cases.
feel: I feel **calm** about work, attentive to freelance income.
S0.quote: Our smallest branch has half the shelf space that our database assumes.
fieldNote: Her **eleven-month reserve** and high pay explain confidence in a mild change.
She uses AI daily but checks **physical shelf space** through a store manager before changing orders.

steps.text: Continue Thursday calls with store managers about unusual stock levels
Test the new allocation feature against last winter overstock cases
Keep transferring money into household savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will automate more forecasting, buying and routine customer answers. That could free planners to solve delivery failures, but the company should not count the saved minutes as a reason to erase people without discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, much of my own screen work is exactly forecasting and checking. I am good at building new workflows, yet a smaller team could also mean fewer management seats. My savings and other local openings help, but my income supports our rent when my partner has a slow month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I’d test the new allocation model on two regions with store managers reviewing every exception. I’d meet our staff council about a written rule for redeployment and paid training. If planners are cut after the system spreads, I’d apply for the open retail-operations manager posts only if the salary covers our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious. I can probably find another role, but I cannot promise my six planners will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the test measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsold stock, empty shelves and how often a manager overrides an order. If the tool looks good only because shops absorb extra pallets, the report is wrong. I would publish the override count alongside sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a smaller team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If work genuinely falls, I would discuss numbers honestly. I would first ask where the planners can move and who pays for the training. A quiet cut after a successful pilot would break trust.

say: **Forecasting and buying** will change; planners should have a say in redeployment.
I’d show **store overrides** alongside sales results.
think: A smaller team could mean fewer **manager posts**, including mine.
My salary steadies our **rent** when freelance work slows.
do: **Test** the allocation model in two regions with manager-reviewed exceptions.
**Meet** the staff council about redeployment and paid training terms.
**Apply** for retail-operations posts if planner jobs fall and pay covers rent.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my team and possible management cuts.
S1.quote: A quiet cut after a successful pilot would break trust.
fieldNote: Her **pilot design** counts hidden shop labour and overrides, not only sales figures.
She has **outside options**, yet her partner’s variable work makes salary conditions important.

steps.text: Test the new allocation model in two regions with store review
Meet the staff council about redeployment and paid training terms
Apply for retail-operations openings if salaries cover household rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team AGI by 2028 could make nearly every buying and planning decision cheaply. We need a plan for workers and a way for stores to challenge a bad automated order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be good at using AI, but if full AGI does almost any thinking work by 2028, that skill alone may stop being scarce. Robots arrive around 2031 for the physical store and warehouse work, while my office could be cut first. I expect the allocation team to shrink and cannot assume my post survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within a month I’d bring a proposal to the staff council for notice dates, severance and store appeal rights. I’d also look at three open supplier-relationship jobs and compare their pay with my current salary before applying. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post is cut, I’d take a real supplier role if offered; otherwise I’d use the household reserve while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed about the speed and the people on my team. Eleven months of savings gives my partner and me choices, but a rapid cut would still turn our lives around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why supplier relationships?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A delayed shipment can involve a factory, a store and a buyer making different promises. I know how to get them into the same call. I do not claim the supplier-relationship job is safe from AGI, only that it is posted today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of the reserve would you spend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would pay rent and basic bills while I searched, not fund a new business on a frightened guess. My partner’s contracts might help, but we would not count an unsigned booking as income. We would review it monthly.

say: **AGI by 2028** requires notice dates and a way to challenge wrong orders.
I’d bring **severance terms** to the staff council.
think: Daily AI skill may lose value when **full AGI** handles thinking work in 2028.
My office could shrink before **robots** reach stores around 2031.
do: **Propose** notice, severance and store appeal terms within a month.
**Compare** three posted supplier roles with my current salary before applying.
**Pay** basic bills from savings only if my job ends.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my own post, and alarmed by the speed and risk to my planners.
S2.quote: I do not claim the supplier-relationship job is safe from AGI, only that it is posted today.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** does not lead her to assume she will be safe under full AGI.
She treats **posted supplier roles** and eleven months saved as options, not guarantees.

steps.text: Bring notice and severance proposals to the staff council
Compare posted supplier roles and apply only if salary is acceptable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn where retail decisions still need a human answer. I want store workers, buyers and planners in the test, not just people who own the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me try a supplier role while my current pay continues. My screen work could still go around 2031, and robots for physical stock work follow around 2034. I can be ready to switch jobs, though I cannot make a future vacancy appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From early 2027 I’d spend one paid day each month with the supplier-relations unit if my director approves cover for my team. I’d keep running the AI allocation tests and let stores record wrong recommendations. After 2031, I’d apply for a supplier manager post only if it exists, pays at least my current salary and still gives me authority to settle disputes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious but not stuck. I can test a new role while building better evidence for the people who actually lift the boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a store worker add to your test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They know when a delivery blocks an aisle or arrives during the only two-person shift. A good sales forecast does not tell us when a delivery blocks a store aisle. I would give them a way to mark each bad order in the test.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on equal pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner’s freelance work is uneven, and my salary pays the fixed bills. We have savings, but I do not want to spend them to make an employer’s transition cheaper. I would take a pay cut only after we made a separate household decision.

say: A **five-year test** should include store workers, buyers and planners.
Stores need a way to flag **bad orders** before new rules spread.
think: My screen role could end in **2031**, before physical-stock robots around 2034.
I can test supplier work, but a future **vacancy** is uncertain.
do: **Spend** one paid day monthly with supplier relations if team cover is approved.
**Record** store reports of wrong AI allocation advice.
**Apply** after 2031 only for supplier posts with equal pay and dispute authority.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with room to test a new role.
S3.quote: A good sales forecast does not tell us when a delivery blocks a store aisle.
fieldNote: She uses a **paid supplier trial** to test a career route while keeping her team covered.
Her **salary floor** protects fixed bills when her partner’s contracts vary.

steps.text: Spend one paid day monthly with supplier relations if cover is approved
Record store reports of wrong AI allocation advice during tests
Apply after 2031 for supplier posts only with equal pay and authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 is enough warning to build a fair transition with store workers at the table. A company that has ten years should publish job paths and pay before asking people to trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me time to manage suppliers or lead a larger retail unit, if those roles remain. My current planning work still faces AGI in 2036, and capable robots in stores and warehouses follow around 2039. My partner and I could also add to our reserve if both incomes hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d continue our monthly savings transfer and make the store-feedback test a normal part of allocation reviews. I’d take a paid two-year rotation through supplier relations if the director offers it without a pay cut. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for a retail or supplier lead post only after checking the salary, team and decision authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the long outcome, but I am not waiting for a perfect prediction. A decade lets us build a route with evidence and real offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the published path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay, training hours and minimum time in each role. A planner with children cannot take an unpaid six-month experiment. I would ask the staff council to check the terms before management announces them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if supplier jobs vanish too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the reserve for ordinary bills while looking at other retail firms, because there are many in this city. I would not tell my team that moving sideways is a sure rescue. We would revisit the plan every year.

say: A **decade** warrants published pay and job paths with store workers involved.
I’d have the **staff council** review training terms.
think: My planning role still faces AGI in **2036**, before store robots around 2039.
A larger reserve and new role depend on **both incomes** and real openings.
do: **Continue** monthly savings transfers and store-feedback reviews in 2026.
**Take** a paid supplier rotation only if offered without a pay cut.
**Review** retail lead roles for salary and authority after 2036.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but able to build evidence and check offers.
S4.quote: A planner with children cannot take an unpaid six-month experiment.
fieldNote: Her **fairness test** includes workers with children even though she has none herself.
Her own **career route** remains conditional on paid rotations, genuine authority and family income.

steps.text: Keep transferring money into household savings each month
Include store feedback in regular allocation reviews
Take a paid supplier rotation if offered without a pay cut
Review retail lead vacancies for salary and authority after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because even a strong team might be cut before stores have a way to challenge machine orders. Notice dates, real severance and paid paths into other jobs would help. I can use my savings; I cannot use them to protect every planner.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the store worker who has to move the extra pallet. A forecast can be accurate on sales and still make somebody’s shift impossible. That worker belongs in the design meeting.

headlineQuote: A forecast can be accurate on sales and still make somebody’s shift impossible.
portrait: **Priya, 27**, is an MBA-trained allocation manager leading six planners at a large home-goods retailer.
She has **high pay**, eleven months saved and many local planning jobs; her partner’s freelance income varies.
She uses **AI daily** but tests forecasts against shelf space, store feedback and workers’ time.
She moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to anxiety about her own post in 2028, then tests supplier work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut planners before stores can challenge wrong automated orders.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **notice dates**, severance and paid routes into other jobs would help.
